As vibe coding becomes increasingly popular, the number of new apps being listed on the App Store is surging, doubling in the first half of 2026, but downloads have only grown by 2%. Details below.

New app listings surge while download growth lags far behind

A report published today by The New York Times, citing the latest data from Sensor Tower, notes that although the number of new apps listed on the App Store doubled in the first half of 2026, downloads grew by just 2%:

The New York Times report also mentions two developers who have been launching vibe coding apps on the App Store. One is Marco Pérez, who plans to leave his job at JPMorgan next month to devote himself full-time to app development; the other is David Svensson, who has launched 11 niche apps over the past five months and treats vibe coding as a hobby rather than a business opportunity.

The report reads as follows:

Mr. Pérez, a software engineer based in Chicago who had never previously developed a mobile app, spent five weeks over the winter tinkering with "vibe coding" AI tools to build prototypes, followed by two weeks preparing the app for release on Apple's App Store. The app, called InfoDrizzle, performed reasonably well, recording 1,300 downloads and earning around US$500. Mr. Pérez's next app proved even more popular. In May this year, he launched Stampa in roughly a week—a scrapbooking app that turns photos into digital stamps. Stampa has been downloaded 20,000 times and earned around US$3,000.

Apple spokesperson Peter Ajemian, responding to The New York Times, addressed another impact of this listing surge: earlier reports indicated that the App Store's review process has come under pressure as a result.

Ajemian said, "Apple has consistently been able to review 90% of app submissions within 48 hours," adding that Apple is "delighted that a new generation of developers is embracing the latest tools to build and ship apps faster than ever before."

He also stated, "All apps must meet the same high standards of quality, privacy, and safety that users have always trusted," regardless of whether they are developed through vibe coding.
